item.title: The TIB Terminology Service and Its Terminology Collection for the Earth System Sciences
item.description:
Anette Ganske, Angelina Kraft, Alexander Wolodkin
ISPRS International Journal of Geo-Information, vol. 15, issue 10, pp. 454
DOI: 10.3390/ijgi15100454
Advancing Earth System Sciences (ESS) depends on our ability to integrate highly diverse data from a range of disciplines, including geographical information sciences, palaeontology, marine science, biodiversity research, atmospheric sciences and biology. A major scientific obstacle to this integration is semantic heterogeneity: different disciplines use different methods and terms to describe data, resulting in fragmented vocabularies. We address this challenge by providing the ESS terminology collection, which is a source of state-of-the-art terminologies for this scientific community. This collection already contains 50 curated terminologies. New terminologies can be suggested by scientists at any time. The ESS collection enables the consistent annotation and semantic alignment of heterogeneous ESS research data. It enhances the FAIR data principles—particularly findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability—thereby facilitating interdisciplinary research and data reuse. This collection enables the ESS community to assess the quality and completeness of ontology metadata and the extent to which their terms comprehensively represent the scientific content of a field.

item.title: From R-Trees to Learned Indexes: A Systematic Review of Spatial Indexing Across 2D, 3D and Point-Cloud Geospatial Query Scenarios
item.description:
Yang Jiao, Suhaibah Azri, Uznir Ujang
ISPRS International Journal of Geo-Information, vol. 15, issue 10, pp. 452
DOI: 10.3390/ijgi15100452
Learned indexes are presented as a new direction for spatial data access, yet their transfer to native 3D geospatial and point-cloud tasks remains unclear. Building on existing reviews and benchmarks, this review connects index structures with geospatial application scenarios, query requirements, and benchmark dimensions. Following PRISMA 2020 reporting guidance, it combines searches of Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore and ACM Digital Library with revision-stage reference checking. After eligibility assessment and consolidation of overlapping reports, all 111 retained studies were included in the qualitative synthesis. The review develops a unified taxonomy of traditional and learned spatial indexes, including hybrid designs, along two analytical dimensions, rule-driven and learning-driven designs, and 2D and 3D data support. The synthesis reveals an imbalance: learned indexes are widely evaluated in 2D and general multidimensional settings, whereas native 3D geospatial indexing remains dominated by traditional and hybrid structures. The review reframes the learned–3D gap as a workload-adaptation and benchmark-standardization problem. Finally, it identifies design requirements and benchmark dimensions for geospatial-aware learned 3D indexes, including density-aware partitioning, geometry-preserving learning, exact–approximate refinement, update-aware maintenance, out-of-core scalability, and system integration.

item.title: Resident–Tourist Differences in Waterfront Recreation During a Peak Summer Week in Hangzhou: An Analytical Framework of Spatiotemporal Behavior and Flow Networks
item.description:
Siming Zheng, Wentao Yan
ISPRS International Journal of Geo-Information, vol. 15, issue 10, pp. 453
DOI: 10.3390/ijgi15100453
Urban waterfronts serve as important recreational spaces for both residents and tourists. However, differences between these groups in recreational behavior and environmental influences remain insufficiently understood. Using mobile phone signaling data from 16–22 July 2021, this study compares resident and tourist waterfront visitation in central Hangzhou during a summer peak-season week. The “behavior–structure–correlates” framework combines spatiotemporal analysis, social network analysis, K-means clustering, and Geodetector. Residents accounted for 81.10% of all recorded waterfront visits, but the resident–tourist composition varied across waterfront systems: tourists contributed 37.95% of visits to West Lake, compared with 17.80% to the Grand Canal and 9.53% to the Qiantang River. Residents showed proximity-oriented and relatively dispersed visitation patterns, whereas tourists concentrated around iconic attractions. The resident recreation flow network was denser than the tourist network, with densities of 0.43 and 0.20, respectively. Core waterfront units function as both major attractions and intermediary nodes, while key paths demonstrate the guiding role of major transport corridors. Metro station availability showed the highest explanatory power for resident visitation (q = 0.226), while surrounding accommodation density ranked highest for tourist visitation (q = 0.307). Interaction analysis further highlighted combinations of waterfront resources and public transport for residents, and urban functional diversity and metro availability for tourists. By linking group-specific behaviors, spatial structures, and environmental correlates, the framework provides empirical support for matching differentiated recreational demands, implementing service-type-based waterfront management, and improving waterfront service efficiency in tourist cities.
